doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Lake Charles roadhouse and naming the Nat Garner Trio
summary: Stopping to eat in Lake Charles, the trio became the six-night house band at Sammy's, named for Nat Cole and Erroll Garner.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: You have to be efficient in a small town, I guess. So you left school in January 1950, and were headed to Houston, but in Lake Charles, Louisiana, you stopped to eat in a local roadhouse, and I guess the quality your wife described of shedding your shyness when it came to asking to sit in or to play, took hold because you became the regular band at the place, with a six­ night-a-week...
Do you remember what kind of place that was?

It was a small dance floor. We got a set of drums for the... Dale Hampton, who was a trombone player. We got a minimum set—snare drum, sock cymbal, whatever. But we played there for six weeks, I think.
And then when you went to Texas, what was that weird club you played in? I mean, I never saw it... There was something about the owner of the club in Texas. What was that story?

Maybe we’ll come upon it. I’ll proceed through the book, because these times are very interesting. The place was called Sammy’s Restaurant and Bar. You played swing music and ballads, “Body and Soul,” “I Can’t Get Started,” “Stardust.” Taylor LaFarge said that you hadn’t started composing by that time, so I don’t have to ask you that question...
And you called yourselves the Nat Garner Trio, after your two musical heroes, Nat
